entries.title: CPU engine with libomp (2 threads)
entries.hypothesis: The installed engine was single-threaded; libomp should let it use more cores.
entries.conclusion: Measured 0.10 tok/s, but Colibri only used 2 threads on the M6 (see threads). Reference point for the GPU steps.

entries.title: Metal GPU backend
entries.hypothesis: Expert math and attention were on the CPU; the GPU was idle.
entries.conclusion: Expert math and attention moved to the GPU; the SSD became the largest cost.

entries.title: Overlap SSD reads with GPU work
entries.hypothesis: Reads and math happen one after the other; overlapping should hide some read time.
entries.conclusion: Small gain within noise on its own; kept because it combines with DIRECT.

entries.title: Uncached SSD reads
entries.hypothesis: Reading around the page cache avoids a copy and enables zero-copy GPU buffers.
entries.conclusion: Faster; Colibri reports DIRECT can be drive-dependent.

entries.title: Metal residency set
entries.hypothesis: Registering resident buffers once should cut per-dispatch GPU scheduling overhead.
entries.conclusion: Attention time fell sharply; GPU scheduling overhead mostly gone.

entries.title: GPU keep-alive spin
entries.hypothesis: A spinning GPU keep-alive should reduce dispatch latency.
entries.conclusion: Faster.
entries.tradeoffs: Uses more power; drop on battery.

entries.title: Best exact combination
entries.hypothesis: The residency set and the spin target different overheads, so they should add up.
entries.conclusion: 0.43-0.44 tok/s, identical text, about 76% of time now waiting on the SSD.

entries.title: 4 SSD readers instead of 8
entries.hypothesis: Fewer readers might reduce contention.
entries.conclusion: Within noise of 8 readers; the SSD is the limit, not the reader count.

entries.title: 2 SSD readers
entries.hypothesis: iobench saturates at 2 readers.
entries.conclusion: No change.

entries.title: 16 SSD readers
entries.hypothesis: More queue depth might help the SSD.
entries.conclusion: No change.

entries.title: Cross-layer expert prefetch
entries.hypothesis: Loading the next layer's likely experts early should hide read time.
entries.conclusion: Hit rate rose to 10% but speed did not; most prefetched loads were discarded.

entries.title: Page cache as the expert cache
entries.hypothesis: Letting macOS cache experts might use free RAM better than slabs.
entries.conclusion: GPU out-of-memory errors on every block; stopped.

entries.title: Expert cache not wired into RAM
entries.hypothesis: Wiring may not matter with a tiny cache.
entries.conclusion: Refused to start: free RAM had dropped to 12.2 GB right after the mmap failure. Inconclusive; retry on a quiet machine.

entries.title: 2 cache slots per layer (RAM 20 GB)
entries.hypothesis: Doubling the expert cache should raise the hit rate.
entries.conclusion: Hit rate 2% to 4%; too small to matter. A useful cache needs tens of GB.

entries.title: CPU-only: 6 threads instead of 2
entries.hypothesis: Colibri uses only the M6's 2 "Super" cores (colibri#2194).
entries.conclusion: CPU math and prompt reading scale with cores.

entries.title: CPU-only: 12 threads instead of 2
entries.hypothesis: Colibri uses only the M6's 2 "Super" cores (colibri#2194).
entries.conclusion: CPU math and prompt reading scale with cores.
entries.tradeoffs: Efficiency cores add heat; 6 vs 12 differences are small.

entries.title: Metal exact: 6 threads instead of 2
entries.hypothesis: Colibri uses only the M6's 2 "Super" cores (colibri#2194).
entries.conclusion: No change: exact Metal runs wait on the SSD.

entries.title: Metal exact: 12 threads instead of 2
entries.hypothesis: Colibri uses only the M6's 2 "Super" cores (colibri#2194).
entries.conclusion: No change: exact Metal runs wait on the SSD.
entries.tradeoffs: Efficiency cores add heat; 6 vs 12 differences are small.

entries.title: Metal skip < 0.5: 6 threads instead of 2
entries.hypothesis: Colibri uses only the M6's 2 "Super" cores (colibri#2194).
entries.conclusion: CPU-side overhead fell from 26% to ~9-12% of each token.

entries.title: Metal skip < 0.5: 12 threads instead of 2
entries.hypothesis: Colibri uses only the M6's 2 "Super" cores (colibri#2194).
entries.conclusion: CPU-side overhead fell from 26% to ~9-12% of each token.
entries.tradeoffs: Efficiency cores add heat; 6 vs 12 differences are small.

entries.title: Skip missed experts below weight 0.03
entries.hypothesis: Skipping low-weight experts that are not in RAM avoids SSD reads.
entries.conclusion: Skipped almost nothing; identical text.

entries.title: Skip missed experts below weight 0.05
entries.hypothesis: Skipping low-weight experts that are not in RAM avoids SSD reads.
entries.conclusion: Skipped almost nothing; identical text.

entries.conclusion: Skipped <1% of loads; identical text.

entries.title: Skip missed experts below weight 0.20
entries.hypothesis: Skipping low-weight experts that are not in RAM avoids SSD reads.
entries.conclusion: ~25% of loads skipped; reworded, still correct.

entries.title: Skip missed experts below weight 0.30
entries.hypothesis: Skipping low-weight experts that are not in RAM avoids SSD reads.
entries.conclusion: ~60% skipped; reworded, still correct.

entries.title: Skip missed experts below weight 0.40
entries.hypothesis: Skipping low-weight experts that are not in RAM avoids SSD reads.
entries.conclusion: ~77% skipped; reworded, still correct.

entries.title: Skip missed experts below weight 0.50
entries.hypothesis: Skipping low-weight experts that are not in RAM avoids SSD reads.
entries.conclusion: ~84% skipped; facts held in a 5-question quiz, instruction following slipped.

entries.title: Skip missed experts below weight 0.70
entries.hypothesis: Skipping low-weight experts that are not in RAM avoids SSD reads.

entries.title: Skip missed experts below weight 1.0

entries.title: Code prompt: skip below 0.20
entries.hypothesis: Check the skip trade-off on a code answer.
entries.conclusion: Same function structure through 0.30; reworded at 0.50.

entries.title: Code prompt: skip below 0.30
entries.hypothesis: Check the skip trade-off on a code answer.
entries.conclusion: Same function structure through 0.30; reworded at 0.50.

entries.title: Code prompt: skip below 0.50
entries.hypothesis: Check the skip trade-off on a code answer.
entries.conclusion: Same function structure through 0.30; reworded at 0.50.

entries.title: Cache-aware routing
entries.hypothesis: Swap low-ranked experts for ones already in RAM.
entries.conclusion: 0% swapped: with ~1 slot per layer there is nothing in RAM to swap to.

entries.title: Cache-aware routing, wider window
entries.hypothesis: A wider window might find more cached experts.
entries.conclusion: Same as default: nothing to swap to.

entries.title: Skip < 0.10 plus cache-aware routing
entries.hypothesis: Combine both lossy levers.
entries.conclusion: Same as skip < 0.10 alone.

entries.title: Vulkan dense chain, experts on CPU
entries.change: VK=1 build, COLI_VULKAN=1 COLI_VK_CHAIN=1 (+ MoltenVK patch)
entries.hypothesis: Keeping whole layers on the GPU avoids per-layer CPU round trips.
entries.conclusion: Expert math stayed on the CPU (71% of time); prompt reading 3x slower.
entries.tradeoffs: Needs MoltenVK and a portability patch.

entries.title: Vulkan chain + 3 GB GPU expert tier
entries.hypothesis: Put routed experts on the GPU too.
entries.conclusion: Only ~3% of experts reached the GPU tier.

entries.title: Vulkan chain + tier, skip < 0.5
entries.hypothesis: Lossy mode is attention-bound, where the chain should help most.
entries.conclusion: Slower than Metal at the same threshold.

entries.title: Vulkan chain + Metal experts, skip < 0.5
entries.hypothesis: Chain for dense work, Metal for experts.
entries.conclusion: Chain attention took 78% of time; prompt reading 154 s.

entries.title: GPU prompt reading
entries.hypothesis: Prompt reading runs attention on the CPU; the GPU should be faster. Not bit-exact by design.
entries.conclusion: Prompt reading time unchanged (23.5 s vs 23.2 s): it is bound by expert reads, not attention. Generation was 16% slower in this single run, but the code-prompt run saw no change, so treat that as noise or as an effect on draft-verify steps. Not worth using.

entries.title: GPU prompt reading, code prompt
entries.hypothesis: Same, with a longer prompt.
entries.conclusion: No change (32.3 s vs 32.2 s).

entries.title: Skip below 0.30 with 12 threads
entries.hypothesis: Lossy runs spend more time on CPU-side work, which more threads should cut.
entries.conclusion: Same speed as 2 threads (the run is still SSD-bound). Marked the usable everyday setting by the owner on 2026-10-18: quality bench v1 found no real mistakes at skip 0.3 (normal style: 23 correct, 1 cut off by the token cap; terse: 24/24), about 2x exact generation speed, and with terse prompts ~52 s per answer vs ~64 s exact.
entries.tradeoffs: Changes output (reworded answers). Validated on 24 graded prompts only.

entries.title: Skip below 0.40 with 12 threads
entries.hypothesis: Lossy runs spend more time on CPU-side work, which more threads should cut.
entries.conclusion: Small gain within noise.

entries.title: Skip below 0.50 with 12 threads
entries.hypothesis: Lossy runs spend more time on CPU-side work, which more threads should cut.
entries.conclusion: Faster: with most reads skipped, CPU-side work is the bottleneck that threads remove.

entries.title: Second SSD for expert reads
entries.hypothesis: Exact runs are SSD-bound; splitting reads across two drives could nearly double read speed.
entries.conclusion: Not run: needs an external NVMe drive.

entries.title: Lossless compressed experts (int4-rans256-g0)
entries.hypothesis: ~24% fewer bytes to read with byte-exact output.
entries.conclusion: Not run: Colibri has the codec but no engine loader yet; CPU decoding would likely cost what it saves.

entries.title: REAP expert pruning
entries.hypothesis: A smaller model raises the cache hit rate.
entries.conclusion: Not run: still 8 experts per token, so bytes per token stay the same; community GLM cards report quality loss at 34%.

entries.title: 3-bit or mixed-precision experts
entries.hypothesis: int3 cuts expert bytes ~25%.
entries.conclusion: Not run: lossy and needs re-converting 409 GB; papers report large losses at 2-bit.

entries.title: Terse prompting ("answer as briefly as possible")
entries.change: prompt suffix: " Answer as briefly as possible. For code, reply with only the code."
entries.hypothesis: Shorter answers finish sooner even at the same tok/s, if accuracy holds.
entries.conclusion: Quality bench v1 (24 graded prompts): exact answers took 64 s on average instead of 281 s (4.4x faster), with ~10 instead of ~98 output tokens. Every config scored 24/24 terse; normal style had 2 genuinely wrong answers at skip 0.5 (see review). Prompt reading (~40 s) is now most of a terse answer's time.
entries.tradeoffs: Answers are short; ask for detail when needed. Generation speed (tok/s) is unchanged: the gain is fewer tokens.

entries.title: Prompt-lookup drafts off (COLI_LOOKUP=0)
entries.hypothesis: Colibri drafts n-grams from the prompt by default (our runs show 1.04 tokens per forward). Each verify reads experts for every drafted row, so on an SSD-bound run a rejected draft costs a full extra set of expert reads; turning it off could be faster, or show the gate already pays for itself (code prompt repeats more n-grams).
entries.conclusion: Planned: runs in the quiet run (`make glm-quiet`) or `glm_lab.py run-planned`.

entries.title: Prompt-lookup drafts off, code prompt
entries.hypothesis: The code prompt repeats more n-grams than the sky prompt, so drafts may pay there even if they cost on sky.
entries.conclusion: Planned: runs in the quiet run (`make glm-quiet`) or `glm_lab.py run-planned`.

entries.title: Stack: skip < 0.5 + 12 threads + drafts off
entries.hypothesis: Combining techniques: on the best usable lossy setting, attention and per-forward overhead dominate, so a wasted verify forward costs relatively more than in exact mode.
entries.conclusion: Planned: runs in the quiet run (`make glm-quiet`) or `glm_lab.py run-planned`.

entries.title: Baseline Colibri dev 16239caa (GGUF for GLM, 412 commits after v2.0.0)
entries.hypothesis: The dev branch is 412 commits past the installed v2.0.0 (bf244291) and touches colibri.c (GGUF reader, QT_GGML/QT_KVB, MTP from a GGUF). Check it does not regress the int4 Metal path before using it for the GGUF experiment below.
entries.conclusion: Planned: runs in the quiet run (`make glm-quiet`) or `glm_lab.py run-planned`.

entries.title: Stack: skip < 0.5 + 12 threads on Colibri dev 16239caa
entries.hypothesis: Does the newer engine move the best usable lossy stack (attention/overhead bound)?
entries.conclusion: Planned: runs in the quiet run (`make glm-quiet`) or `glm_lab.py run-planned`.

entries.title: int8 MTP draft head for GLM-5.3
entries.hypothesis: Our glm-5.3 container has no MTP head ("MTP absent"). Colibri reports 2.2-2.8 tokens per forward when it pays. On an SSD-bound run a 3-row verify reads more experts (2% hits), so exact-mode gain is uncertain; output stays identical (only verified tokens are kept).
entries.conclusion: Planned: needs `make glm-prep-mtp` first (downloads the FP8 shards holding layer 78 from zai-org/GLM-5.3 and converts the head to int8, ~10 GB on disk; the owner's model folder is not touched). Then the quiet run picks it up.
entries.tradeoffs: ~10 GB more on disk; the head's dense part stays resident (its experts stream like the others), so some RAM leaves the expert cache.

entries.title: Stack: MTP head + skip < 0.5 + 12 threads
entries.hypothesis: In lossy mode each forward is dominated by attention and overhead, not SSD, so fewer forwards per token (MTP) should compound with skipping.
entries.conclusion: Planned: needs `make glm-prep-mtp` first.

entries.title: GLM-5.3 as a 2-bit GGUF (Unsloth UD-IQ2_M, 239 GB)
entries.change: Colibri dev 16239caa + unsloth GLM-5.3 UD-IQ2_M GGUF (imported)
entries.hypothesis: The 2-bit GGUF is ~239 GB against ~419 GB for the int4 container, so roughly 40% fewer expert bytes per token (~7 GB instead of 12.7 GB): exact-mode SSD ceiling ~0.9 tok/s instead of ~0.5, and lossy skip runs read less too. Risk: Colibri computes GGUF blocks (QT_GGML) on the CPU only, with no Metal copy, so the math may eat the I/O saving; NEON kernels exist. The GGUF carries the MTP (nextn) layer, which Colibri dev turns on.
entries.conclusion: Planned: needs `make glm-prep-iq2m` first (~239 GB download, imported to ~/colibri-models/glm-5.3-iq2m). Lossy: needs the quality bench before any use.
entries.tradeoffs: Lossy (2-bit experts); CPU-only expert math for GGUF blocks; a second 239 GB model on disk.

entries.title: Stack: 2-bit GGUF + skip < 0.5 + 12 threads
entries.hypothesis: Fewer bytes per expert and fewer experts read should multiply; tests how far the stack goes before compute dominates.
entries.conclusion: Planned: needs `make glm-prep-iq2m` first. Lossy twice over (2-bit and skipping): quality bench required.

entries.title: GLM-5.3 as a 3-bit GGUF (Unsloth UD-IQ3_XXS, 282 GB)
entries.change: Colibri dev 16239caa + unsloth GLM-5.3 UD-IQ3_XXS GGUF (imported)
entries.hypothesis: The quality-safer middle ground: 282 GB vs 419 GB int4 (~33% fewer expert bytes), top-1 agreement 84.2% and KLD 0.27 per Unsloth (2-bit: 78.5%, 0.45). Same CPU-only caveat for GGUF blocks; the GGUF carries the MTP layer.
entries.conclusion: Planned: needs `make glm-prep-iq3xxs` first (~282 GB download). Lossy: quality bench required.
entries.tradeoffs: Lossy (3-bit experts); CPU-only expert math for GGUF blocks.

entries.title: Stack: 3-bit GGUF + skip < 0.5 + 12 threads
entries.hypothesis: The best-quality low-bit file with the best lossy stack on top.
entries.conclusion: Planned: needs `make glm-prep-iq3xxs` first. Lossy twice over: quality bench required.

entries.title: GLM-5.3-Flash (321B) on the glm53 engine
entries.change: convert zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash with tools/convert_glm53.py (int4-g64, ~195 GB out, ~25 h), run with coli chat
entries.hypothesis: Same expert shape as GLM-5.3 but 45 layers (42 MoE) and hidden size 4096: ~4.8 GB of int4 expert weights per token instead of ~12.7 GB (-62%). Exact SSD ceiling ~1.3 tok/s, and lossy skip runs could approach the 5 tok/s target. It is a different, smaller model, so the owner decides whether it counts toward the mission.
entries.conclusion: Planned, manual: the glm53 engine has none of our speed settings (no PIPE, DIRECT, DEGRADE_ZERO, OMP sizing; it has GLM53_EXPERT_GB, COLI_METAL, COLI_MODEL_MIRROR) and prints speed as "decode N token in X s = Y tok/s", which the lab parser does not read yet. Fast route instead of the 25 h conversion: `make glm-prep-flash` (Unsloth UD-IQ3_XXS GGUF, ~120 GB, read in place by Colibri dev), then a manual timed run. The GLM-5.3 stack does not carry over as is; it needs Flash-specific settings.
entries.tradeoffs: Smaller model, likely weaker answers than the 744B GLM-5.3.

entries.title: Check the Qwen models' architecture (dense vs MoE)
entries.change: read config.json of Qwen3.8-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B
entries.hypothesis: Artificial Analysis lists Qwen3.8-27B as 3B active, Colibri says dense; expert streaming only helps a MoE.
entries.conclusion: Read from the official config.json files. Qwen3.8-27B is dense: Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration, 64 layers, hidden 5120, one MLP per layer (intermediate 17408), no experts, so all ~27.8B weights are used for every token (Ollama: 27.8B, NVFP4). Artificial Analysis's "3B active" for it is wrong. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B is a MoE: Qwen3_5MoeForConditionalGeneration, 40 layers, hidden 2048, 256 experts with 8 routed plus 1 shared per token (expert width 512). Routed experts per token are ~1.0B parameters (~0.55 GB at int4 gs64), so expert streaming applies to it and not to the 27B.

entries.title: Qwen3.8-27B (dense) through the installed Ollama MLX model
entries.change: Ollama qwen3.8:27b-mlx fully in RAM; quality bench (normal, terse) in two settings: exact (thinking off, temperature 0, 128 tokens, comparable with GLM) and native (Ollama defaults: thinking on, model sampling, up to 4096 tokens)
entries.hypothesis: Published intelligence 34 vs GLM-5.3 45, but it fits in RAM: likely tens of tok/s, so far more correct answers per minute.
entries.conclusion: Ready and queued in the lab app (bench qwen38-27b-ollama: exact + native, normal + terse), after the skip-0.4 re-run, when the machine has been quiet for 2 min. glm_bench.py compare puts it next to GLM: correct answers, waiting time, correct per minute.

entries.title: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (MoE, ~3B active) with every expert in RAM
entries.hypothesis: Upper bound for the small MoE on this Mac; Colibri reports 6.0 tok/s CPU and 9.9 tok/s integrated-GPU Vulkan elsewhere.
entries.conclusion: Planned: needs ~23 GB download (make glm-prep-qwen36) and a qwen36 adapter for the bench tools.

entries.title: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B at simulated 8 / 16 / 24 GB machines
entries.hypothesis: A MoE reads only ~1.5 GB of experts per token, so it should stay usable on 8-16 GB machines where a dense model cannot.
entries.conclusion: Planned: after sm-qwen36-a3b-resident. Simulated: a RAM cap does not reproduce a slower SSD (~3 GB/s on base Macs).

entries.title: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B: Vulkan expert tier (MoltenVK) vs CPU
entries.change: COLI_VULKAN=1 with the MoltenVK portability patch, engines/ clone
entries.hypothesis: The qwen36 engine has no Metal backend; Colibri's Vulkan tier helped an integrated GPU (9.9 vs 6.0 tok/s).
entries.conclusion: Planned: after sm-qwen36-a3b-resident.

entries.title: Dense Qwen3.8-27B on Colibri at 16 / 24 GB profiles
entries.hypothesis: Contrast case: a dense model must read most weights from the SSD every token once it does not fit, ~13.5 GB per token.
entries.conclusion: Planned: needs a Colibri conversion of Qwen3.8-27B (~56 GB source download).
